turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, Mrs Keane, take the chair near the desk. I'm Dr O'Connell.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm jaded already. That car park has me fit to be tied.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Siobhan, her daughter. I live in with her and I sort the pill box. The ankles have her in foul form.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not in foul form. I'm tired. Sit down and stop narrating me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. What brought you in, from your side?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The ankles are like puddings, and I'm puffed just getting to the gate.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Swelling's been three weeks. No, scratch that, it came on after the ramipril was stopped, so about six weeks.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): If you say so. I don't be writing down my ankles.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So six weeks of swollen ankles, and breathless on the flat to the gate. Is there a cough with it now?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The cough went when they took me off that yoke. Good riddance.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain when you get puffed?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes. Not really.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll not mark that as a yes, so. Do you wake gasping in the night?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I sleep, when the legs aren't throbbing.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's up to the loo once or twice a night. I'd say that's the water tablet.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll do the tablets properly in a minute. Any fever, or shivers?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. Just tired. Fierce tired, if you must know.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired as well, noted. Let me see the legs before the boxes come out.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pitting oedema, both sides, up to the mid-shin. Chest is clear, I don't hear crackles. Pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-two, pulse seventy-six and regular.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the pressure desperate?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): The pressure's grand, actually. The swelling is what I want to chase. Siobhan, talk me through the box, proper names if you have them.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mornings, the water tablet. I was about to say forty milligrams, but no, the box says twenty. Furosemide twenty.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Furosemide twenty milligrams, once each morning?
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's the plan. Mm, I suppose she takes it. Most mornings. If I'm at the shops I can't swear it isn't still sitting in the Monday slot.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I take the blasted thing. Don't make me out to be dopey.
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You do, mostly. Then there's the little white one. Amlodipine, five milligrams.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): And the blood pressure tablet. The other little white one. You always forget that.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mam, there isn't another one. The little white one is the amlodipine. I hope to God I haven't been dropping two into the box.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll count a single amlodipine five milligrams once a day. Not two. You've been on blood pressure treatment for years, is that right, and the amlodipine is for that?
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Years, yes. Since before I moved back in.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Years. I'm sick of hearing about it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else in there?

[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): A small pale yellow tablet with the breakfast. Label's destroyed, got wet on the sink, and I cannot tell you the name of it. It's not the water one and it's not the white one.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then it stays unnamed. I'd rather a blank than a wrong guess. What did the other doctor stop?
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ramipril, five milligrams. The hospital doctor stopped it because of a dry cough.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): That was two months back. No, wait, about six weeks, the same time Siobhan says the ankles started.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ramipril five, stopped about six weeks ago, cough settled since. Allergies, anything that doesn't agree with her?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing. How many times do I have to say it.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Penicillin, Mam. You came out in a rash with it when I was small, and you've steered clear of it ever since.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I did not. That's a yarn.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll record that you recall none, and Siobhan remembers a penicillin rash from years back. We won't be using penicillin today either way. Any painkillers from the chemist?
[SEG0042] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Paracetamol, the odd time, for the legs. Not every day, and I wouldn't put a dose on it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): The odd one. I don't want a pile of new tablets.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through out loud. The ankle swelling could be the amlodipine, that one is well able to cause swelling, or it could be fluid retention. I am not calling this heart failure. I won't conclude that today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So you've no idea, in other words.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I've two things it might be, and one thing I'm not saying. What I will change is the water tablet, for the swelling: furosemide up from twenty milligrams to forty milligrams, by mouth, every morning.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Forty instead of the twenty. Same tablet.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Same tablet, new strength. If you go dizzy, or the swelling takes off, ring the surgery. And when you redo the box, one amlodipine only, don't double it.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): More of the water tablet. Grand. Lovely.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll also have bloods this week, kidney function and the salts, seeing as we're increasing the diuretic.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her to the nurse for that.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): The drive over was a pure nuisance. Stuck at the bridge, rain belting down.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I was telling her about Aoife's camogie, the under-tens. Soaked to the skin and they still got the win.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Two points she scored, then nothing would do her but chips. A terror.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair play, camogie in that rain. My nephew's the same with the hurling, comes in plastered in muck and delighted with himself.
[SEG0056] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She wants a pink helmet now. We spent Saturday in the sports shop trying on every single one.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): The price of a pink helmet. Don't start me.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the helmets. I want to see you back here in two weeks, swelling and the blood results.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, if the car park doesn't finish me.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the breathing worsens before then, or you can't get your air lying down, don't sit on it. Come back or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0061] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll keep an eye, and I'll sort the box tonight once the chemist has the new strength.

[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Prescription will be at reception. Just to hand it back to you: swelling about six weeks, cough gone since the ramipril stopped, furosemide from twenty to forty each morning, amlodipine five once and not twice, yellow tablet still with no name, penicillin not agreed between you, bloods this week, review in two weeks.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the lot. I'm wore out. Are we done?
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): We're done. Mind the step.

spec.situation: Older patient with a live-in carer or daughter who manages the pill box; names of tablets are described ('the little white one', 'the water tablet'), one was stopped by another doctor, one is double-counted. Doctor reviews and changes one medicine.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
